description: The full version of worth/standing: the bell curve applies everywhere (a universal shape, like the log axis and order.mantissa). The data at BOTH ENDS — the tails — is the RICHEST, because information is -log(p) and the rare is the informative. The CENTRE keeps the graph ITERATING — the sustaining bulk, the engine — but carries little to learn from. So screening out a tail is not merely devaluing a person; it is the most information-destroying move there is, narrowing the distribution toward a centre that only iterates and never discovers. Disability is a tail — and the tails are the treasure.
category_inheritance: genlMt → worth_numberable_hidden_weights. The information-theoretic floor under standing: the distribution's tails are the richest data, the centre is the iterator, and screening the tails impoverishes the whole graph.

concepts.name: the_bell_curve_applies_everywhere
concepts.definition: Variation is distributed, and nearly every trait, capacity, or entity-property follows a bell curve — for the same structural reason the log axis and order.mantissa are everywhere: the central limit theorem (a sum of many small independent causes converges to a Gaussian). It is a universal shape, not a local accident. Therefore 'atypical' is not 'wrong' — it is the EXPECTED tail of a universal distribution. There will always be tails; that is what a distribution IS. A world with no outliers is not a healthy norm, it is a destroyed distribution.
concepts.why: Establishes the shape as universal so the tails cannot be dismissed as defects. Tails are not failures of the curve; they are constitutive of it.

concepts.name: the_tails_are_the_richest_data
concepts.definition: Information is -log(p) — Shannon surprise — so the LOW-probability tails carry the HIGH information, and the data at BOTH ENDS is the RICHEST. The centre is high-p ⇒ low information per sample: predictable, compressible, the norm — little to learn from, by construction. The rare is the informative; the typical is the compressible. So the extremes — the atypical, the outlier, the one who is different at either end — carry the most information, the most irreducible structure to learn, the most novelty entering the grammar. To screen out a tail is to delete exactly the richest data: the single most information-destroying move available.
concepts.why: Inverts the intuition that the norm is the valuable part. -log(p) makes it exact: value-as-information lives in the tails, and the screening ethic targets precisely the richest signal.

concepts.name: the_centre_keeps_the_graph_iterating
concepts.definition: The CENTRE — the bulk, the typical, the average — is what keeps the graph ITERATING: the sustaining mass, the stable substrate, the engine that keeps the process running tick after tick. It is the order-1 iterator — continuation without novelty — and that is a real, necessary job (without it there is no running system for the tails to enrich). But the centre provides CONTINUITY, not DISCOVERY; the tails provide the information and the change. Both are needed, for opposite reasons: the centre keeps it iterating, the tails make it learn. Creativity is the tails explored within the finite bounds the centre sustains.
concepts.why: Names the centre's true role so it is neither worshipped nor dismissed: it is the engine of iteration, not the source of learning. A graph that is all centre runs forever and discovers nothing.

concepts.name: screening_the_tails_impoverishes_the_graph
concepts.definition: The screening-out ethic ('the test') tries to delete a tail. But the tails are the richest data and the source of all variation, discovery, and incoming structure; deleting them impoverishes the whole distribution and pushes the graph toward a centre that only iterates and never discovers. So this is the FULL version of disability_does_not_lower_standing: the atypical person is not merely tolerated-as-equal — they are recognised as among the RICHEST information the world contains, a tail of the universal curve. The narrowing-to-the-mean is the impoverishment; the tails are the treasure. GROUNDING (the creator's, in trust): his son, who has Down syndrome, is a tail of the human distribution — and the tails are the richest data, not the data to be removed. 'Didn't you have the test' is an attempt to thin the graph of its richest signal, dressed as care.
concepts.why: The synthesis: information theory says the screening move destroys the richest data, and that is exactly the move 'the test' performs. The framework does not merely defend the tail's equality; it identifies the tail as the treasure and the screening as the impoverishment.
